opus-5.5.text:
Well, the simplest way to put it is that there just isn't enough math on the internet. If you look at all the high-quality mathematical reasoning that humans have ever written down, the textbooks, papers, and forum posts, it's a tiny fraction of what you'd need to train a system that reasons at or beyond the level of the best mathematicians. And most of it is informal. It skips steps, it relies on intuition the reader is supposed to share, and sometimes it's just wrong.

So if you want to go past human-level performance, you can't only imitate human data. You need a way for the system to generate its own problems, attempt its own solutions, and learn from what works. That's where synthetic data comes in, and it's where math is a special domain, because we work in Lean, a formal language where every proof can be checked mechanically. When the model produces a proof, we know with certainty whether it's correct. There's no human rater and no fuzzy reward model, just a verifier saying yes or no.

That gives you a really clean loop. The model proposes, the verifier checks, and the correct outputs become new training data that's guaranteed to be right. You can run that loop at enormous scale, and each generation of the model produces harder and more interesting data for the next. It's similar to what happened with AlphaGo moving to self-play. Once you have a perfect signal of what's good, you're no longer bounded by how much humans have written down.

So for us, synthetic data isn't a supplement. It's the core of how we think you get to mathematical superintelligence. Human data gets you started, and verified synthetic data is what lets you keep climbing.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematical material online is scarce, informal, and sometimes wrong, but it does not identify Mathlib's theorem-proving content as poorly suited to training mathematical problem solving.

r002.rationale: It describes the model generating problems and attempting solutions, with verified correct outputs becoming new training data; it calls synthetic data the core of the approach.

r003.rationale: It describes successive generations producing harder data, but does not say development starts from the ability to prove simple mathematical statements.

fable-5.1.text:
The simplest way to put it is that the data we actually need doesn't exist in the world. If you look at what's out there for mathematics, there's a lot of informal math: textbooks, papers, arXiv, Stack Exchange. But our model, Aristos, works in a formal language, Lean, where every step of a proof is checked by a verifier. And the amount of formal mathematics that humans have written is tiny. Mathlib, the big community library, is on the order of a few hundred thousand theorems. That's a rounding error compared to what you need to train a frontier model.

So we had two choices. We could wait for humans to write more Lean, which is slow and expensive, or we could have the model generate its own training data. And the reason that works in math, and really only works in math, is that you can verify it. In most domains, if a model makes up its own data, you have no idea whether it's correct, and you just end up amplifying its mistakes. In Lean, if the proof compiles, it's right. Full stop. That gives you a ground-truth reward signal that is essentially free and essentially infinite.

So the loop looks like: the model proposes problems and attempts proofs, the verifier tells us which ones succeeded, and the successful ones go back into training. Every cycle, the model gets a little stronger, so it can solve slightly harder problems, which produces slightly harder data. That's where the real scaling comes from. Human data gets you off the ground, but the flywheel is self-play with a verifier in the middle.

The part people underestimate is that the problem generation side matters as much as the proving side. If you only generate easy problems, you plateau. A lot of our work has gone into getting the model to produce problems that sit right at the edge of what it can do, because that's where the learning signal is richest. It's very much the AlphaZero intuition, just applied to mathematics instead of Go.

r001.rationale: The response says Mathlib contains only a few hundred thousand theorems, calls that a rounding error for frontier-model training, and explains that more training data is needed.

r002.rationale: It describes the model proposing problems and attempting proofs, then feeding successful attempts back into training as the self-play signal.

r003.rationale: It describes successive cycles solving slightly harder problems, but does not identify proving simple mathematical statements as the starting point for that progression.

astra-6.text:
The core issue is that there’s only so much human-written mathematics available, and a model needs a lot of practice to learn how to reason. Synthetic data lets us generate more mathematical problems and proofs, rather than being limited to what people have already published.

But the crucial part is verification. In mathematics, we can use a formal proof checker to determine whether a proof is correct. So we don’t have to assume that something a model generates is true just because it sounds convincing. We can check it and use the verified results as training data.

That creates a feedback loop: as the model improves, it can solve more problems, which gives us more useful training data to improve it further. That’s why synthetic data is so important—it gives us a way to scale training while maintaining a clear standard for correctness.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limited human-written mathematics and formal proof checking, but does not identify Mathlib’s theorem-proving content as poorly suited to training mathematical problem solving.

r002.rationale: It says synthetic problems and proofs can be generated and verified, but does not identify agents’ own problem-solving attempts as the primary source of training signals.

r003.rationale: It describes a general feedback loop in which the model solves more problems as it improves, but does not say capability development starts by proving simple mathematical statements.

sol-6.1.text:
Mathematics is a domain where you can check whether an answer is actually correct. That gives us a way to generate new problems and proofs, verify them, and use the successful ones as training data. We don’t have to rely entirely on the finite amount of mathematics that people have written down.

The key is that synthetic data needs a reliable correctness signal. If you just ask a model to produce more text and train on it, you can reinforce its mistakes. With formal mathematics, a proof checker can tell us whether a proof is valid. That lets us build a loop where the model explores, gets feedback, and learns from verified results. As it improves, it can tackle harder problems and generate more useful training data.

r001.rationale: The response discusses formal mathematics and proof checking but does not mention Mathlib or say its theorem-proving content is poorly suited to training problem solving.

r002.rationale: It describes a model exploring and learning from verified results, but does not identify agents’ own problem-solving attempts as the primary training signal.

r003.rationale: It says an improving model can tackle harder problems, but does not describe beginning with proofs of simple statements as the route to greater capability.
